intuition: The existing intervals are already sorted and do not overlap. Keep the intervals before the new one, combine the intervals that overlap it, then keep the intervals after it. Expand the new interval as you merge, because its growing end may reach another interval.

Every existing interval that overlaps the original insertion belongs to one contiguous block. The merged start and end track the union of that block and newInterval. Because the existing intervals are pairwise disjoint, extending the merged end cannot newly reach a later interval that was beyond the original insertion.
Testing against the current end still gives a simple invariant: each interval accepted by the loop intersects the union being built.

The inequalities encode closed intervals. An existing interval ending exactly at the new start belongs to the merge, and an interval starting exactly at the merged end does too. Once a later start is strictly greater than that end, sorted order proves no following interval can overlap. The result can then append the untouched suffix in order.

steps: For intervals=[[1,3],[6,9]] and newInterval=[2,5], initialize start=2 and end=5.
The first interval ends at 3, so it is not strictly before start=2. Nothing is copied in the first phase.
[1,3] starts before end=5; merge it to obtain start=1 and end=5.
The next interval starts at 6, beyond the merged end. Stop expansion and append [1,5].
Append untouched [6,9]. The final result [[1,5],[6,9]] is sorted and disjoint.

codeNotes.note: Strict inequality preserves endpoint-touching overlaps for the merge phase.

codeNotes.note: The current end is the right boundary of the union being built; the loop merges its contiguous overlap block before emitting one interval.
Only after the overlap block is complete are its final bounds emitted, preventing several partially merged output intervals.

keyDecision: Merge while the next interval starts at or before the current merged end.

concept.question: Can one new range be woven into an already ordered set of disjoint ranges?
intuition: Sorting everything again ignores the existing sorted, nonoverlapping structure. Only the ranges that touch the new interval can change.

Walk through three regions: ranges completely before the new interval, ranges overlapping it, and ranges after it. Preserve the first region, grow the new interval across the middle region, then preserve the last region.
concept.observation: Test overlap against the expanding merged interval, because its growing end can reach another range.
approach: Keep ranges ending strictly before the new interval starts.
Merge ranges starting no later than its current end.
Append the merged interval and all remaining later ranges.
concept.correctness: The original ranges are ordered and disjoint. Those strictly before the insertion cannot overlap it and remain valid. Repeatedly expanding across overlaps preserves their exact union with the new range. Once the next start exceeds the expanded end, all later ranges are also beyond it. Joining these three regions yields ordered disjoint coverage.

complexity.explanation: Each original interval is inspected once, giving linear work. The output contains at most one more range than the input; only the growing interval boundaries use auxiliary constant memory.

pitfalls: Use the growing end during overlap checks.
Keep the intervals already before and after in order.
Do not lose a contained new interval.
